issues.legal_issue: A pending review application does not become infructuous merely because judicial administration and the governing court structure change while it is pending.
material_facts: A review application was pending when the former state judicial administration was replaced by a common High Court and the former High Court legislation was repealed.
The successor legislation continued proceedings pending in the former High Courts, and the successor High Court had jurisdiction to hear a restored appeal.
issues.conclusion: The review application remained maintainable; if review were admitted, the restored appeal could be continued and decided by the successor High Court under the law then governing it, without confirmation by the former ruler or another authority.
issues.legal_principle: The continuation provisions in clause 8 of Ordinance II of 1124 and section 8 of Act V of 1125, together with sections 25 and 26 of Act V of 1125 and articles 214 and 225 of the Constitution, preserved the proceeding and supplied the successor High Court's jurisdiction. The requirement for confirmation under sections 11 and 12 of Regulation IV of 1099 did not make the proceeding ineffective after the judicial changes; even if section 12 applied, section 11 applied only as far as possible.

predicates.review_proceeding: A party sought review of a court judgment.
predicates.review_pending_during_judicial_transitio: The review proceeding remained pending when the judicial administration and governing court structure changed.
predicates.successor_court_continues_pending_procee: The new judicial arrangements continued pending proceedings in a successor court.

issues.definition: When a review proceeding is pending during a judicial transition and the successor court continues pending proceedings, the review proceeding remains maintainable.

issues.legal_issue: Review is confined to the specified grounds, and a reason beyond those grounds must be at least analogous to them to qualify as another sufficient reason.
material_facts: The applicants sought review of an appellate judgment, alleging apparent errors and other sufficient reasons.
The review provisions in the applicable civil procedure code were similar in terms to Order 47, rule 1 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908.
issues.conclusion: The review court had limited jurisdiction: review could be allowed only for discovery of qualifying new evidence, an error apparent on the face of the record, or another sufficient reason analogous to the specified grounds.
issues.legal_principle: The Travancore Code of Civil Procedure, in terms similar to Order 47, rule 1 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, fixes definitive limits on review. “Any other sufficient reason” means a reason at least analogous to the grounds specified in the rule, as held in Chhajju Ram v. Neki and Bisheshwar Pratap Sahi v. Parath Nath, and adopted in Hari Shankar Pal v. Anath Nath Mitter.

rule.if: review_proceeding and (qualifying_new_evidence or apparent_record_error or analogous_sufficient_reason)

predicates.review_proceeding: A party sought review of a court judgment.
predicates.qualifying_new_evidence: The applicant relied on new and important evidence that due diligence could not have enabled the applicant to produce earlier.
predicates.apparent_record_error: The judgment contained an error apparent on the face of the record.
predicates.analogous_sufficient_reason: The applicant showed another reason sufficient on grounds at least analogous to the specified review grounds.

issues.definition: In a review proceeding, qualifying new evidence, an apparent record error, or an analogous sufficient reason permits review.

issues.legal_issue: Failure to determine an important issue on which the claimant's title and entitlement to relief depend is an error apparent on the face of the record.
material_facts: The suit sought possession of church properties on the basis that the claimants had been validly elected as trustees.

The validity of the meeting at which the claimants were said to have been elected was disputed, including whether competent persons convened it and whether the churches entitled to notice received notice.
The trial court had found defects concerning the conveners and notice, but the appellate majority did not effectively determine those issues, which bore on the claimants' title.
issues.conclusion: The appellate judgment's failure to effectively determine the important issues about the meeting's validity was an error apparent on the face of the record and supported review.
issues.legal_principle: Under the review provision corresponding to Order 47, rule 1 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, a judgment's failure to deal effectively with an important issue on which the claimant's title and the suit's maintainability depend is an apparent error. In an ejectment suit, the claimant must establish title by its own strength.

predicates.review_proceeding: A party sought review of a court judgment.
predicates.judgment_omits_important_issue: The judgment did not effectively decide an important issue raised for determination.
predicates.issue_determines_claimant_title: The unresolved issue affected whether the claimant had title and could maintain the claim for possession.

issues.definition: In a review proceeding, omission of an important unresolved issue that determines the claimant's title permits review for apparent error.

issues.legal_issue: A court's material misconception that a party made a concession, or of the concession's scope, is a sufficient reason for review analogous to an error apparent on the face of the record.
material_facts: The appellate majority treated counsel as having conceded that one side had not left the church and relied on that understanding when it did not determine matters bearing on the parties' respective positions.

An affidavit and accompanying correspondence were placed before the appellate court alleging that counsel had made no such concession and had instead advanced a connected legal submission about both sides.
The Supreme Court found that the appellate judgments had been misled by a misconception about the nature and scope of the alleged concession.
issues.conclusion: The alleged misconception about the concession was a sufficient reason, analogous to an error apparent on the face of the record, for allowing review; the affidavit could be relied on to establish the alleged misconception.
issues.legal_principle: Under the review provision corresponding to Order 47, rule 1 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, a court's mistaken assumption that a concession was made, or its misunderstanding of a concession's terms or scope, is a sufficient reason analogous to an apparent record error. Such an error may not appear in the judgment record and may be brought to the court by affidavit. The Court relied on Sha Mulchand & Co. Ltd. v. Jawahar Mills Ltd., Madhu Sudin Chowdri v. Musammat Chandrabati Chowdhrain, and Rekhanti Chinna Govinda Chettiyar v. S. Varadappa Chettiyar, and distinguished the concern discussed in Reg. v. Pestanji Dinsha where no affidavit had been filed before the court whose record was challenged.

predicates.review_proceeding: A party sought review of a court judgment.
predicates.court_misconceives_concession: The court treated a party as having made a concession, or misunderstood its terms or scope, and relied on that understanding.
predicates.affidavit_supports_actual_position: An affidavit was presented to the court whose judgment was challenged to explain the position actually taken.

issues.definition: In a review proceeding, a material misconception about a concession supported by an affidavit permits review for an analogous sufficient reason.

issues.legal_issue: Deciding a case against a party on matters outside the issues on which the parties went to trial is an error apparent on the face of the record.
material_facts: The parties had agreed that a general issue about the full extent of an ecclesiastical authority's powers need not be decided, leaving specific powers for determination.

The appellate majority nevertheless relied on matters that were not pleaded or included in the issues for trial, including the extent of authority to decide matters of faith and whether approval was required for an appointment.
issues.conclusion: The appellate majority's reliance on matters outside the issues on which the parties went to trial amounted to an error apparent on the face of the record and supported review.
issues.legal_principle: Under the review provision corresponding to Order 47, rule 1 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, deciding against a party on matters outside the issues on which the parties went to trial is an error apparent on the face of the record.

predicates.review_proceeding: A party sought review of a court judgment.
predicates.judgment_relies_on_unpleaded_matters: The judgment relied on matters that were not pleaded by the parties.
predicates.matters_outside_trial_issues_affect_deci: Those matters were outside the issues tried and affected the decision against a party.

issues.definition: In a review proceeding, reliance on unpleaded matters outside the trial issues that affect the decision permits review for apparent error.

issues.legal_issue: A claimant seeking possession in an ejectment suit must succeed on the strength of the claimant's own title, not on the weakness of the opposing party's case.
material_facts: The claimants sought possession of church properties on the basis that they had been validly elected trustees.
The opposing party's alleged separation from the church did not itself establish the claimants' title as trustees.
issues.conclusion: The claimants had to establish their own title as trustees; defeating the opposing party's claim alone would not entitle them to possession.
issues.legal_principle: The established rule for an ejectment suit is that the plaintiff must succeed on the strength of the plaintiff's own title and not on the weakness of the defendant's case.

predicates.ejectment_suit: The proceeding sought recovery of possession from an opposing party.
predicates.claimant_seeks_possession: The claimant sought possession based on an asserted right or title.

issues.definition: In a proceeding seeking possession, the claimant must establish the claimant's own title.
